Chapter 1
ERIC ROBERTS LAITHWAITE
Algebra is widely used
in Engineering. for
example in building
high speed trains.
[Born: 1921 - Died: 1997]
Known For: the "Father of Maglev"
Eric Roberts Laithwaite was a British
electrical engineer, known as the "Father
of Maglev" his development of the
linear induction motor and maglev rail
system. The first commercial maglev
(magnetic levitation) train in 1984 in
Birmingham. It travelled 600m at only
42km/h. Today the fastest Maglev train
can reach 603km/h (375mph).
Equations,
Expressions,
Inequalities
and Identities
This Chapter covers the following........
• recognise and solve equations in r which are quadratic in some function of z
e.g. 2*-5x?+5 for k =2
• find the discriminant of a quadratic trinomial az*+br+c and interpret the
nature and the number of real roots of the related equation f(z) = ax?+br + c
• complete the square for a quadratic function and use the solution to
determine the turning point (vertex) of a graph of a quadratic function and
sketch the graph
find the equation of a graph (quadratic) given sufficient information
• solve quadratic inequalities in one unknown
• interpret the difference between identities and equations and use identities
to determine unknown coefficients in polynomials
• find the equation of a graph (cubic) given sufficient information

Addition and Subtraction of Surds
We can add and subtract surds only when they are in the simplest form and
we can only add or subtract like surds. When two surds can be expressed
with the same surd factor (the root part must be the same), they are said to be
like surds, otherwise they are said to be unlike surds. For example, 3/5 and
-8/5 are like surds, and 3/2 and 2/3 are unlike surds.

terms from one side to another. Both sides are simplified independently until
they are in the same form.

2.1 Sequences and Series
Introduction
In Ordinary Level, we learnt that a Sequence is a list of numbers. Any time
you write numbers in a list format, you are creating a sequence. The numbers
may have been generated randomly (numbers obtained while tossing a die)
or generated by a rule (the list of even numbers starting at 2). Each number in
the sequence is called a term. The "..." at the end of the sequence show that
the list of numbers could go on indefinitely, i.e. the sequence is infinite.

Recognise Arithmetic and Geometric Progressions
In an Arithmetic Sequence/Progression (AP) successive terms are always
formed by always adding (or subtracting) the same value to one term to get to
the next term. This number added to each term in an arithmetic sequence is
called the "common difference", d, because if you subtract the values of any
two consecutive terms you will always get the same answer. Eg: 2, 5, 8, 11,...
and 3, -1, -5, -9,... are arithmetic, since 3 and -4 respectively are added in
each case. [Note: adding -4 is the same as subtracting +4, i.e. +(-4) = -(+4)]

In a Geometric sequence/progression (GP) successive terms are formed by

This number by which each term in a geometric sequence is multiplied, is
called the "common ratio", r, because if you divide the values of any two
consecutive terms you will always get the same answer.

Chapter 2 Sequences. Series and the Binomial Theorem
C. Arithmetic and Geometric Series
A series is simply adding the terms (the sum of the terms) in a sequence.
For example, suppose we have the sequence: I, I,, Ig.... In The series we
obtain from this is: T, +I, + Iz t... +I, and we write s, for the sum of these
terms. Thus, whenever one hears the word 'series', the first thing to come to
mind is the fact that the terms are being added. It is the sum of the numbers.
If the series stops after a finite number of terms it is called a finite series.
E.g. 2 + 4 + 6 + 8 + 10 is a finite series of 5 terms. If the series does not stop
but continues indefinitely it is called an infinite series. E.g. 2 + 4 + 6 +... is an
infinite series. An arithmetic series involves adding the terms of an arithmetic
sequence and a geometric series involves adding the terms of a geometric
sequence.
The Sum (S.) of an Arithmetic Series
The sum of an arithmetic series is found by multiplying the number of terms by
the average of the first and last terms.

Chapter 2 Sequences. Series and the Binomial Theorem
E. Sum to Infinity of a Convergent Geometric Progression
In sequences of the type 2, 6, 18, 54,.. where consecutive terms have a
common ratio bigger than 1, the sum of these terms tends to infinity. That is,
as we add the next term, the sum just gets larger and larger without bounds.
This is an indication that the series diverges. The same will happen in a
sequence where the common ratio is smaller than -1.
The value of the common ratio cannot be equal 1 because then the series
would not be geometric and the sum formula would involve division by zero.
So, r ‡ 1. When the common ratio is between -1 and 1 (-1 < r < 1), the terms
become smaller in size as we continue along the sequence. We call the sum
of such a geometric sequence a convergent sum, because as we add the next
term the sum converges upon a number (tends towards a definite limit). In
other words, if you keep adding the terms of the sequence together forever,
you will get a finite value. This value is equal to: Sx= 1 -r

The Binomial Theorem
n! and (.) Notation
To obtain the coefficients of (a + b)", where n is any positive integer, we can
extend Pascal's Triangle up to row n if n is small. However, in Pascal's
Triangle, you need the to know numbers in the previous row in order to obtain
the numbers in the next row. When n is large, it would be too tedious to
evaluate all the previous rows of the triangle. The notations, n! (read as
"" factorial') and (") (read as 'n choose r') are used to ease the process of
finding the coefficients.
We define n factorial, denoted by n!, as:
n Factorial: n!
n!= nx (n-1) x (n-2) x...x 1 where n is a positive integer.
E.g.: 4! = 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24 and 5! = 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 120
Note: 0! = 1 and 1! = 1

The range of the inverse function is equal to the restricted domain of the original function.
Finding the Domain and Range using only the Formula
If you have to find the domain of a function and only the formula is given with
no restrictions then you must avoid the following:
• division by zero
• square roots of negative numbers
These numbers are not in the domain, but all the other numbers are in the
domain (x E R).
The easiest way to determine the range of a function when only the formula is
given is to find the inverse of that function and then determine the domain of
the inverse. The domain of the inverse function will then be equal to the range
of the original function. Notice however, that the domain consists of z-values,
and the range consists of y-values.

In a coordinate system, distances and lines can be represented by algebraic

learnt how to calculate the length of a line segment, find the midpoint of a line
segment, work out the gradient of a line segment and calculate the equation

Angles can be measured in two different units. The most common unit used in
school Mathematics is degrees. The symbol for degrees is °, for example 1°.

angular measurement is known as circular measure. Radians are
represented by the symbol "rad." or byc, for example 1 rad. or 1c. It is applied
especially to those branches of mathematics which involve differentiation and
integration of trigonometrical ratios. The radian (mode 'rad") is sometimes
referred to as the natural unit of angular measure.

4.2 Trigonometry
A.
Graphs of Sine, Cosine and Tangent Functions
The trigonometric graphs are functions. They are used to relate the angles
of a triangle (0) to the lengths of the sides of a triangle (sin0, cos0, tan 0).
They are defined as functions because for every input value (0) there is only
one output value (e.g. sin 0). Therefore the ordered pair (0, sin 0) can be
graphically represented on the Cartesian plane.
Graphs of y= sinx, y= cosx and y = tanx
Many properties of the trigonometric functions can be seen from their graphs.
To draw the graph of a trigonometric function (for a specified interval of
angles), we construct a table of values first, then plot the points and join them
with a smooth curve.
Let's look at the graph of y = sin x for 0° ≤x ≤ 360°. A table of values for
plotting the graph is shown below.

The graph of y = sin x oscillates up and down. The maximum value of sin x
is 1 when x = 90° and the minimum value is - 1 when x = 270°. So, the range
of values of sin x for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360° is - 1 ≤ sin x ≤ 1. Half of the difference
between the maximum value and the minimum value of the graph is called the
amplitude of the graph. The graph of y = sin x has an amplitude of 1.
This sine curve repeats itself every interval of 360°(2T). A function that
repeats forever is called a periodic function. The length of the interval over
which the curve repeats itself is called the period.

Chapter 4 Circular Measure and Trigonometry
Trigonometric Graph Sketching
In the introduction, the graph of the trigonometric function y = sin x was
plotted accurately on graph paper. However, the information required by some
questions may not require us to make an accurate drawing of the graph, but
only a sketch of the graph showing the essential features of each function.
REMEMBER
How to Sketch Trigonometric Functions
* Use a pencil and ruler and draw the x- and y-axes. Make your axes at least 10 cm.
* Determine and write down the important features of the sketch
- the maximum and minimum points of the function
- the.r - intercepts (y = 0) and y - intercept (x = 0) if the graph crosses the axes.
- the period (indicating when the graph repeats itself over a certain interval)
- the amplitude, the height from the centre line
- determine any asymptotes, if so, draw them in with a dotted line
* Plot all the information and draw the curve, with the knowledge of the shape of the
basic function.

pages.text:
Chapter 4 Circular Measure and Trigonometry
Proving Identities
You will be given two expressions with a modified equal (=) between them.
These expressions are already equal to each other but you are asked to
prove that they are equal. The end goal of any trigonometric identity proof is
to make the LHS of the equation and the RHS of the equation look the same.
However, this must be done with extreme caution, because only one side of
the identity can be changed at a time. So, we cannot use methods such as
squaring, taking roots on both sides or cross multiplication. Due to the fact
that we work with only one side at a time, we can only use techniques that we
would use in simplifying expressions.
REMEMBER
Proving of Identities - Hints
• Terms or factors of each expression cannot be moved to the other side of the equal sign.
• Should squares occur, try to rewrite them using the Pythagorean "Square" Identities.
• Express all the remaining functions in terms of sin 0 and/or cos 0, using reciprocals
and quotient identities.
• Now try to simplify by means of factorising, cancellation or addition of fractions using
the LCM.
• Sometimes it is necessary to multiply the expression (LHS or RHS) by 1, an
expression that will give the difference between two squares, i.e. x1+ cos 0
1 + cos 0 °
• Look out for expressions such as sin? 0 + cos' 0, sec' 0 - tan? 0, cosec? 0 - cot2 0,
sin 0 cosec 0, cos 0 sec 0 and tan 0 cot 0 because they are all equal to 1.
• Start to simplify the expression on the most complex side and simplify it so that it has
the same form as the simplest side. You can also manipulate both sides until the
final expressions are the same on both sides.

A trigonometric equation is an equation containing a trigonometric function

5.1 Introduction to Vectors
5.1 Introduction to Vectors
In Ordinary Level Mathematics we studied two dimensional vectors. In this
chapter you will be reminded about vectors in 2-dimensional space, before
being introduced to vectors in 3-dimensional space.
Recall that a vector is a quantity which has
magnitude (size) and direction. The length of
direction
A
the line shows its magnitude and the arrowhead
shows the direction. Therefore, vectors are only
about magnitude and direction, the position
is irrelevant. The arrow from L to M is the same
magnitude (length)
B
length and has been drawn in the same direction as
M
the arrow from A to B. This means that the points A and L have been
displaced or translated by the same vector to B and M, respectively. The
arrow AB and the arrow LM represent the same displacement or vector.
A. Standard Notations of Vectors
Notation using Upper Case
A displacement from A to B is written as the vector AB
. In the notation AB ,
the order of the letters is important. It indicates that A is the initial or starting
point and B is the terminal or ending point. The vector BA is different from
the vector AB
, their magnitudes are equal but they are in opposite directions,
AB = - BA
In the diagram above, AB = LM. Even though the lines and
arrows are drawn on different parts of the diagram, the displacement shown by
each is the same.
Notation using Lower Case
Sometimes lower case letters are used for vectors. In text, it can be shown in
bold type, for example, a or b. In written work (with a pen or pencil), vectors
are shown as a or b (underlined letter).
The vectors a and b have the same direction but not the
same length, so vectors a and b are parallel but not equal.
In fact, a is half the length of b, therefore b = 2a.
Vector c is
3 of the length of vector b, but in the opposite direction, therefore
c =3b. A number (usually) used to scale a vector is called a scalar. So in
'2a' the vector a is being multiplied by the scalar 2.

differentiate you get acceleration. So, differentiate position to get velocity, and

G. Maxima and Minima Problems
We will now look at some problems involving maximum and minimum values.
For example, the manufacturers of milk containers often need to minimise the
cost of manufacturing their product. To do this they need to find the minimum
amount of material required to make a container for a given volume. Other
situations might involve finding the maximum area that can be enclosed within
a certain shape.
The first step in all of these problems should be to read the problem very
carefully. Once you have done that, the next step is to identify which
quantity is to be optimized and which is the constraint (the limiting quantity).
One quantity will be clearly indicated as having a fixed value and therefore it
must be the constraint. Once you have identified the constraint, the quantity
to be optimized should be fairly simple to determine.

7.1 Indefinite Integrals
7.1 Indefinite Integrals
A. Integration as the reverse of Differentiation
In chapter 6 you studied differentiation, which is the first basic tool of
calculus. In this chapter you will learn about integration, which is the second
basic tool of calculus. Integration is the reverse process of differentiation,
i.e. the operation you carry out to undo differentiation. Therefore, we call this
reverse process antidifferentiation. Just as differentiation has a graphical
aspect, the gradient of a curve, integration has a graphical aspect, the area
under a curve.
Integration has many uses; for example, planning spacecraft flight paths,
deriving cost functions in economics, modelling real-world behaviour for
computer games and even in the design of soles of some shoes.

"+3" is 3 units away from zero,
and "-3" is also 3 units away from zero.
So the absolute value of +3 is 3,
and the absolute value of -3 is also 3.
In some situations, for example the determination of estimation errors, we are
concerned mainly with the numerical value of a quantity and not its sign. So,
we define the numerical value of a real number x to be its modulus or its
absolute value, which is denoted by |x |. Therefore, to show that we want the
absolute value of something, we write "I" marks on either side. They are called
"bars". It is important to note that the modulus of any number (positive or
negative) is always a positive number, so in practice to find the "absolute
value" means remove any negative sign which is in front of a number. We
define the modulus function, also called the absolute value function, as follows:

In Ordinary Level, we learnt that Polynomials are algebraic expressions
which consist of terms in the form ax" where n is a non-negative (i.e. zero or
positive) integer and a is a real number and is called the numerical coefficient

Linear and quadratic expressions are examples of polynomials. Remember
that polynomials cannot contain terms involving fractional powers or negative
powers of the variable. For example 2' . 3 + 4zt is not a polynomial, because
the second term involves division by the variable x and the third term
contains an exponent which is not a whole number.
The highest power of x (the variable) in the polynomial is called the degree
of the polynomial. For example, 4x' + 5x'- 2x + 7 is a polynomial of the third
degree. In this section we will revise how to use long division to divide a

8.2 Polynomials
B. The Remainder Theorem
In the previous section, we learnt how to use long division to find the
remainder when a polynomial is divided by another polynomial. We will now
learn another method to find the remainder when a polynomial is divided by a
linear divisor, without going through the process of long division.
In Example 15, we did the following long division, x+4
22°-I and found:
(2X3-X)=(2x'-8x+31)X(x+4) +(-124) - → Remainder: -124
If we make the divisor equal to 0 (x + 4 = 0) and substitute x =- 4 into the
polynomial we get: P(-4) = 2(-4)3 - (-4) =-124 So, we can find the remainder
without doing any division. So: if P(x) = 2x3-X
then P(-4) = -124 (the remainder)
In general:
If a polynomial P(x) is divided by a divisor D(x) = (x - c) to give the Quotient
Q(x) and a remainder R, then: P(x)=(x-c)Q(x)+ R.
If we make the divisor equal to 0 (x - c = 0) and substitute x = c into the
polynomial we get: P(c)=(c-c)Q(x)+R
P(c) =(0)Q(x)+R
P(c) = R
The Remainder Theorem
If a polynomial P(x) is divided by (x - c), the
remainder is P(c).
If a polynomial P(x) is divided by (ax - b), the
remainder is P(i).

Chapter 8 Algebra
C. The Factor Theorem
In the previous section, we learnt that if a polynomial P(.r) is divided by a linear
divisor (x - c), D(r), then the Division Algorithm for Polynomials states that
P(J)=(x-c)Q(x)+R or P(x)= D(r)Q(x) + R
and the Remainder Theorem states that the remainder R = P(c).
But if the remainder R = 0, then P(c) =0 and P(x)=(x-c)Q(r), i.e. (I-c) is a
factor of P(x).
In general:
The Factor Theorem
If a polynomial P(x) is divided by (x - c) and
P(c) = 0 then (x - c) is a factor of P(x).
If a polynomial P(x) is divided by (ax - b) and
P(i) = O then (ax -c) is a factor of P(z).
The Factor Theorem is a special case of the Remainder Theorem when the
remainder is equal to zero (R = 0). We can use the Factor theorem to find the
factors of a polynomial and hence solve cubic equations.
Example 21: Show that (x-2) is a factor of x-x-6.
Solution:
Let f(x) = x3-X-6
f(2) = (2)-(2)-6
= 8-2-6
= 0

A.
Graphs of Exponential Functions
We learnt to solve exponential equations and natural exponential equations in a
previous section. In this section we will study the graphs of the exponential
function y = a", where a is a positive constant and a ‡ 1 (if a = 1 the graph will

properties of exponential and natural exponential functions.
Outcome: Learners will be able to sketch exponential and natural
exponential functions and determine the properties of these
graphs.
We will do this investigation using The Geometer's Sketchpad.

on this Investigation scan the QR code or follow the link:

using the equation y = ma: + c, where m is the gradient and c is the y-intercept.

10.1 The Cosecant, Secant and Cotangent Ratios and Graphs
10.1 Cosecant, Secant and Cotangent Graphs
You have already learnt about the ratios cosecant (cosec), secant (sec) and
cotangent (cot).

Now we will look at their graphs. The functions (cosecant, secant and
cotangent) are the reciprocals of the sine, cosine and tangent functions. For
example, whenever the sine is zero, the cosecant will be undefined, so there
will be a vertical asymptote. Whenever sine reaches its maximum value
of 1, cosecant will reach its minimum value of 1; whenever sine reaches its
minimum value of -1, cosecant will reach its maximum value of -1.
Whenever sine is positive but less than 1, cosecant will be positive but
greater than 1; whenever sine is negative but greater than -1, cosecant will
be negative but less than -1. These same principals can be applied for the
secant and cotangent functions.

JAMES BLACK
Many equations used in
chemistry were derived
using calculus, and these
often-involved natural
logarithms.
Further
Integration
[Born: 1924 - Died: 2010]
Known for: Analytical Pharmacology
James Black was a pioneer in the mathematical
analysis of pharmacological models for drug
development. He created the first Beta-Blocker
medicine which treated heart disease.
Mathematical analysis of pharmacological models
is becoming increasingly relevant for drug
development. Emphasis on mechanistic models
has grown and qualitative understanding of
complex biological systems has improved a great
deal.

facilitate the integration of functions such as cos't

13.1 Locate Approximately a Root of an Equation
13.1 Locate Approximately a Root of an Equation
Recall from Ordinary Level that the roots of an equation are the x-intercepts.
When you are asked to solve an equation, you are being asked to find the
roots. Up to now you have solved linear equations, quadratic equations and
even cubic equations by using direct algebraic methods. Equations that are
not reducible to one of the above-mentioned cannot be solved by general
algebraic techniques. This means that most equations arising from
practical applications cannot be solved algebraically. So, if we exchange the
traditional idea of finding exact solutions to equations with the idea of rather
finding approximate solutions, a whole new world of possibilities opens up.
With such an approach, we can, in principle solve any algebraic equation.
This approach is called the numerical method and it is a way of calculating
approximate solutions to equations. Numerical methods are widely used in
engineering, computing, finance and many other applications. In this chapter
we will focus mainly on finding the numerical solution of an equation using an
iterative formula.
Graphical and/or Sign Change Approach
In this chapter we consider only real value solutions of equations. In
general, a given equation has more than one root (solution). It is also difficult
and sometimes impossible to know beforehand how many roots there will be,
or even to get an idea of the values of the roots. A preliminary
investigation is thus necessary to obtain as much information about the
solutions (roots) as possible. For this, graphing is a valuable tool. To sketch
the graph of a function y = f(x) try to determine the following points:
intersection with the y-axis and x-axis (where known)
• maximum and minimum points (turning points)
The change of sign approach focuses on decimal search. Decimal search is
based on the principle that f(x) [the 'y' value] changes sign as a curve passes
through the x-axis at a root.
Above the x-axis, f(x) is positive and below the
x-axis f(x) is negative. Using this principle,
Real
Root
+У
values of f(x) are initially found and then successive
values are found in increments of 0.1 until a change
in sign is found. If further accuracy is required,
successive values could then be found in increments
of 0.01 and 0.001, until a change of sign is found, thereby giving one root of
the equation.

Tribute to Dr. Japie van Zyl
Son of Africa, Man of the Universe
I started writing this book in February 2019. On one occasion, my husband asked, "Why
don't you put something about Dr Japie van Zyl in your book? It would be a motivation for
young Namibian students to realise there are no limits to what can be achieved, even for
someone who was born in Outjo, right here in Namibia". My plan was to contact
Dr Van Zyl as soon as the evaluation process of the textbook was concluded, to ask him to
write a few words of encouragement to Namibian students which could be included in the
Textbook. A week before the evaluation results were released, the devastating news of his
untimely passing shattered the idea. However, motivated by his unwavering spirit and
successful career, I decided to continue anyway and would like to share some of
Dr Japie's favourite quotes. In a message of condolence to his wife, Mrs Kalfie van Zyl and
the entire family, President Hage Geingob said Dr Japie van Zyl had made the complex
field of space science and his work at NASA accessible to many young Namibian learners
and dared them to dream through his exchanges with them.
I hope that these words will motivate and inspire you to achieve great things in your future.
'No country can compete internationally without a solid base of science
and engineering'
'If you have a dream pursue it, but it will demand hard work and
perseverance'
'Do not try and impress your teachers or parents, but compete against
yourself to always keep improving'
'Dream big and big dreams can come true'
I conclude with Dr. Japie's legacy and favourite quote:
'Do not go where the path may lead, go instead where no path is, and
leave a trail: Ralph Waldo Emerson.
